newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela keen to break severance reform deadlock.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela keen to break severance reform deadlock.

text.p: Despite union and private sector intransigence, the Venezuelan government is determined to reform the current system of severance payments and create a private pensions system employed successfully in other countries, Development Minister Freddy Rojas Parra said.

"We have a commitment to reform it (severance payments). It is difficult to say when with these attitudes...But there is the political will to do it," Rojas Parra told Reuters in an interview late Thursday.

Rojas Parra, who sits on a presidential commission studying the reform of the severance payments system, said a consensus proposal made by President Rafael Caldera two months ago was immediately rejected by union leaders and recently thrown out by the private sector.
"The government cannot go to Congress with a proposal to reform severance payments if it does not have sufficient support or backing."
An alternative to Venezuela's severance pay system has been sought for years.
Under the current system, a worker receives a month of his current salary for each year worked. The payment is doubled if a worker is sacked.
Businesses find the system costly while labor has found that it discourages employers from raising wages and encourages them to rotate staff on a regular basis.
"It is a limiting factor for the private sector and for the worker since it stops him from earning more," Rojas Parra said.

The Labor Ministry is currently working on a new proposal which links reform to the creation of private pension funds. The creation of a pension system along the lines of Chile's would boost the local stock market and encourage saving.
"I know that the financial sector has been ready to work on this (private pension funds) for some time," he said.
But first it will be necessary to break entrenched views. "We are in a kind of circle. This circle has to be broken at some point," he said.
